summary: The GLA 250 e is Mercedes-Benz Australia's cheapest plug-in hybrid and the only plug-in grade in a GLA range that is otherwise 48-volt mild-hybrid petrol — it pairs the GLA 200's 1.3-litre four with a motor inside the eight-speed dual-clutch for 160kW/450Nm and 65km of WLTP electric range from an 11.5kWh usable battery. At $78,800 before on-road costs for the MY27 update it still undercuts the petrol GLA 250 4MATIC it out-torques and sits below the $80,809 luxury car tax threshold entirely, but it is a run-out design: the all-new GLA due in Australia in 2027 is electric or mild-hybrid only, with no plug-in successor announced. The compromises are concentrated in long-distance use: a 35-litre tank and a 1.3-litre engine rated at 6.6L/100km with the battery empty give it roughly 595km of combined range, the least of any premium plug-in SUV in this dataset, and the battery takes 50 litres out of the boot.
pros: 65km of electric range is genuine WLTP, not the NEDC figure Mercedes Australia has been caught publishing elsewhere — it sits inside Mercedes' own European 63-70km WLTP band for the facelifted GLA 250 e and matches the UK car's 39 miles, so unlike the GLC 350e's much-quoted 132km this number survives the check, and it covers a typical Melbourne commute on grid power

At $78,800 before on-road costs it lists about $2,700 below the MY27 petrol GLA 250 4MATIC ($81,527) while making more torque (160kW/450Nm against 165kW/350Nm), and it sits $2,009 under the $80,809 ordinary luxury car tax threshold so no LCT is payable at all — its 1.2L/100km combined label also qualifies it for the $91,661 fuel-efficient threshold, leaving roughly $12,800 of options headroom before LCT could ever start
28g/km of CO2 on the combined cycle is far inside Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car limit, so stamp duty is charged at the flat green rate rather than the ordinary tiers
1800kg braked towing is strong for a compact plug-in: the BMW X1 xDrive25e manages 1700kg, the Cupra Formentor VZe 1500kg, and many small PHEVs are not rated to tow at all

Mercedes-Benz Australia's five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional and not tied to servicing inside the dealer network, and the $78,800 price includes metallic paint, 18-inch alloys, heated front seats and a 360-degree camera as standard
cons: The 1.2L/100km label collapses the moment the battery is flat: ADAC lists 6.6L/100km on the WLTP cycle with the battery empty, Parkers recorded 36mpg (7.9L/100km) from the 1.3-litre four on a motorway cruise and called it thirstier than a VW Tiguan eHybrid — a buyer without home charging is running a 1.8-tonne premium SUV on premium unleaded

The battery under the boot floor cuts luggage space from 435 litres in the front-drive petrol GLA to 385, the smallest boot in the range — and carsales, CarExpert and other Australian spec pages still print the petrol car's 435-445-litre figures against the plug-in, so the number most buyers will see is the wrong one

A 35-litre fuel tank leaves roughly 595km of combined range at ADAC's 6.6L/100km battery-empty figure — well short of the GLC 350e's 900km and the BMW X1 xDrive25e's 780km, so it needs refuelling as often as it needs recharging

Charging is AC-only and slow: 3.7kW is standard and takes most of a working day from flat, the 11kW three-phase upgrade is an $800 option, and there is no DC capability at all, so the electric range cannot be usefully topped up away from home

At $78,800 it is above the $75,000 FBT cap and PHEVs lost the FBT exemption entirely on 1 April 2025, so there is no novated-lease advantage left — and the all-new GLA arriving in 2027 drops the plug-in hybrid, which leaves this outgoing car exposed on resale
